q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) AS CNT FROM PRODUCT) SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT CNT FROM CTE)

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. In Q1, the GROUP BY clause uses column position 1 (CUSTOMER_ID), which is valid in some SQL dialects but not standard SQL. In Q2, the GROUP BY explicitly names CUSTOMER_ID, which is more standard. More importantly, Q1 groups by the first column of the SELECT list, which could be ambiguous if the SELECT list had more than one column. However, the real difference is that Q1 may not be valid in all SQL implementations due to GROUP BY position syntax, while Q2 is unambiguous. More critically, Q2 uses a CTE to avoid subquery re-evaluation per group, which could lead to performance differences but not correctness in this case. However, the real issue is that Q1 may not work as intended in some systems, and there is no clear reason for the difference in results. A counterexample is provided below.
